recipe: Slow-roast lamb shoulder with anchovy, garlic & rosemary
servesNote: 8 portions from a 2.7 kg joint — five on Saturday night at ~175 g each, then 210–285 g each for Sunday's three, and enough spare that Sunday dinner for two needs nothing bought for it. ⭐ Maria cooks this alone on Saturday; Karl is out until evening.
adaptations: ⏰ WORK BACKWARDS FROM DINNER — this is the only timing that matters. To eat at 7:00 pm: joint home BY 11:30 am · 11:45 unwrap, salt, oven on to 170°C/150°C fan · 12:45 into the oven covered · 5:15 UNCOVER, oven up to 220°C/200°C fan · 5:45 out to rest, gravy and veg now · 6:30 potatoes and carrots in at 200°C · 7:00 eat.
⚠️ IF THE SHOP RUNS LATE, push the whole column back — do not shorten the covered stage. The joint is forgiving about total time and unforgiving about being cut short.

⛔ BUY THE BIGGEST SHOULDER ON THE SHELF. Bone-to-meat ratio varies enormously on this cut and weight is a poor predictor of yield — if there is a choice, take the one that looks meatiest, not the one closest to 2.7 kg.

⭐ SUNDAY IS THREE PEOPLE EATING THIS AGAIN, and that shapes Saturday: HOLD BACK 250–300 ml OF GRAVY deliberately, make more than Saturday needs, and store the leftover meat submerged in its juices. Reheat covered at 150–160°C with the reserved gravy over it, 20–25 min, and stop the moment it is hot through. ⛔ No air fryer, no skillet, no re-crisping — those tested worst and dry it out.

ingredients.prep: ⛔ Tesco, Saturday morning — the biggest on the shelf
⛔ NOT the jarred chopped garlic — see prep 4
⭐ half into the slits, the rest chopped into the gravy
1.5 kg in large chunks for roasting
4 halved lengthways for the bed, the rest in batons
3 sliced into THICK DISCS for the bed
boiled 4 minutes right at the end
⚠️ WEAKER than the packet says — 300 ml in the tin, the rest for the gravy

equipment.item: The largest roasting tin you own
equipment.why: ⛔ check the joint fits BEFORE the oven goes on
⛔ potatoes and carrots cook separately — crowding the lamb tin steams everything grey
⛔ paper against the meat, foil over the tin. Not foil alone
⭐ testing — the fork decides when it is done, not the clock
the gravy, and the jug goes in the freezer to set the fat

equipment.item: A container the leftover meat fits in WITH liquid around it

equipment.why: over the loose foil tent during the rest

prep: ⭐ UNWRAP THE JOINT THE MOMENT IT IS HOME and pat the whole surface dry with kitchen paper. A wet surface will never brown. Salt it generously all over — about 1½ teaspoons — and leave it on the counter while the oven comes up. This is not about bringing it to room temperature, which does nothing over a cook this long. It is so the salt starts working and the surface dries further.
Heat the oven to 170°C / 150°C fan / gas 3.

Peel and slice 3 onions into thick DISCS — discs, not chunks — and lay them across the base of the tin with 4 carrots halved lengthways. Add a few bay leaves and a couple of rosemary sprigs. ⭐ This bed is not a garnish. It lifts the joint clear of its own rendered fat so the underside roasts instead of deep-frying, and it becomes the body of the gravy later.

Make 10–12 slits in the joint, top and underside, about 2 cm deep. Into each one push a sliver of fresh garlic, a small piece of anchovy fillet and a few rosemary needles. ⛔ Fresh garlic cloves, never the jarred chopped garlic — jarred is packed in liquid, it leaks straight back out of the slit, and its sour note concentrates rather than mellows over a long cook. ⭐ The anchovies are the single best thing in this recipe and they will not taste of fish — over five hours they dissolve completely and leave savoury depth through the inside of the joint. Use about half the tin; the rest goes in the gravy.
Rub the outside with oil, a little more salt and plenty of black pepper. Sit the joint on the onion and carrot bed, fat side up.

steps.text: Pour 300 ml of WEAK chicken stock into the tin — around the joint, never over it. ⚠️ Make the stock weaker than the packet says. This is the most common way the dish is ruined: a litre of strong stock gives you a litre and a half of thin fatty liquor that tastes of stock cube instead of lamb. The liquid is insurance against a scorched tin and a little help with heat transfer. It is not a braising medium.

⛔ Lay greaseproof paper DIRECTLY on the meat, then foil over the whole tin, crimped tight around all four edges. The paper layer is not fussiness: foil touching wet acidic meat for five hours welds to the surface and tears the crust off when you pull it away, and acid against aluminium in a hot oven pits the foil into the juices. There is vinegar and mint sauce in this dish. Use the paper.

⭐ Into the oven for 4½ hours. Then leave it alone. ⚠️ Every time the door opens you lose heat and add roughly 20 minutes. Do not baste, do not check, do not peek. The tin is sealed and the steam inside is doing everything basting would.

Take the foil and paper off. Oven up to 220°C / 200°C fan and give it 30 minutes uncovered to crisp the fat cap. ⭐ The blast comes at the end, not the beginning: browning at the start colours meat while the fat cap is still solid; browning at the end crisps fat that five hours have already rendered. ⚠️ Look in the tin before you turn the heat up — if it has gone dry, add 150 ml of water. A tin that scorches at 220°C turns every drop of the gravy bitter.

⭐⭐ Test it with a FORK, not a clock. The fork should meet no resistance at all — it should turn in the meat like it is turning in butter. With a thermometer, 90–95°C in the thickest part away from the bone. THE MOST IMPORTANT THING ON THIS CARD: if it feels tough, it is NOT done — it is not overdone. This cut gets tougher before it gets tender; between about 60°C and 70°C the collagen contracts and squeezes out water but has not yet turned to gelatin. Cooks panic here and pull it out. Give it another 45 minutes covered and test again. ⛔ Stopping around 70°C is the worst possible outcome — worse than either end.

Rest it 30–45 minutes on a warm dish, tented LOOSELY with foil and a tea towel over the top. ⚠️ Loosely. Tight foil on a crisped fat cap softens it back to flab within fifteen minutes. The rest is not really about juices redistributing — it lets the gelatin firm up so the meat holds together when you pull it, and buys the half hour needed for gravy and vegetables.

While it rests — potatoes and carrots. Oven to 200°C. Cut 1.5 kg potatoes into large chunks and the remaining carrots into batons, toss in oil and salt, roast 30 minutes. ⛔ In a SEPARATE tin. Crowding them into the lamb tin means everything sits in released liquid and steams grey. Green beans on to boil for 4 minutes right at the end.

The gravy. Tip the tin's contents through a sieve into a jug and stand the jug in the freezer for 15 minutes so the fat sets into a layer you can lift straight off. ⭐ You will pour off 200–400 ml of fat from a joint this size, and not doing it is the commonest way this gravy goes wrong — not rich, just greasy. Mash the softened onion and garlic through the sieve as you go; that is the body, and you want the juice, not the pulp. Set the tin over low heat with about a tablespoon of the reserved fat, stir in 5 tsp plain flour and cook until it turns golden, scraping every scrap of fond off the base. Add the de-fatted juices a little at a time, back to the boil between each addition, or it goes lumpy. Top up with weak stock to about 700 ml. Chop the remaining anchovies very finely and stir them in. Simmer two minutes.

⭐ OFF THE HEAT, stir in ONE sachet of mint sauce. Taste. Add a second if it needs it. Off the heat, and at the very end: five hours of cooking has flattened every high note in this dish and the acid is what brings it back — but added early it thins the gravy's body and the mint cooks away to nothing. ⚠️ Hold back 250–300 ml of this gravy for Sunday before it reaches the table.

Pull the meat apart with two forks rather than carving it. It will not slice cleanly and it is not meant to. ⭐ Leftovers go into the container coated in or submerged in their juices, sealed — not dry on a plate under clingfilm. The fat sets on top and seals it, and the gelatin that made this tender today melts again tomorrow.
